claims.feature: hostile: class snobbery in speech; overworked cadences
claims.claim: Stimpson reads character language as class snobbery and Manlove hears overworked cadences and monotonous pitch, hostile readings Shippey and Rosebury rebut.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Literary reception of The Lord of the Rings'

claims.feature: corpus: three lexical causes of archaicity
claims.claim: Siepmann's corpus study finds the impression of archaicity comes from overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense rare or obsolescent words.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation into The Lord of the Rings' (Corpus Linguistics 2017, Birmingham)
claims.quote: the avoidance of words associated with the modern world

claims.feature: corpus: nineteenth-century key words in four sets
claims.claim: Siepmann finds dense nineteenth-century key words in landscape, position/direction (whither, thither, yonder, afar), warfare, and descriptive verbs and adjectives.
claims.quote: obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing

claims.claim: Siepmann shows Tolkien borrows words from his own Beowulf translation (valour, valiant, corslet) and stretches them to new uses like 'lightning smote'.
claims.quote: borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf

claims.feature: corpus: modern words in nineteenth-century patterns; descriptive verbs
claims.claim: Siepmann finds modern core words used in nineteenth-century patterns ('a black smoke') and an abundance of manner-laden descriptive verbs like gleam, loom, plod and stride.
claims.quote: use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns

claims.feature: corpus: dialogue share and hobbit viewpoint
claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann find about half the book is dialogue, verse or embedded story, and narrative adopts the hobbits' viewpoint about 85% of the time.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021)
claims.quote: About half of The Lord of the Rings consists of dialogue

claims.feature: non-standard speech marks Sam and Gollum; epic style for heroes
claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann note Sam and Gollum are marked by non-standard speech while omniscient passages shift to epic style marking Aragorn as an old-style hero.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' and 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann)
claims.quote: marked out by their non-standard speech

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann's book treats key words and collocations, narrative syntax, points of view, landscape, speeches, storytelling, poems, and language and character as separate stylistic systems.
claims.source: Google Books, 'Tolkien as a Literary Artist' (Kullmann & Siepmann, 2021)
claims.quote: The Narrative Syntax of The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Robbins argues Tolkien's phonology and phonaesthetics were applied directly to the various English prose styles of the book, not only to invented languages.
claims.source: Susan Robbins, 'Beauty in Language: Tolkien's Phonology and Phonaesthetics...' (CEEOL abstract)
claims.quote: the various prose styles of English used in writing

claims.claim: Halbrooks shows the narrator's voice changing with setting, cheerful near the Shire and later sounding like an historian, nature writer or epic poet.
claims.quote: like an historian, or a nature writer, or an epic poet

claims.claim: Halbrooks reads 'Concerning Hobbits' as nineteenth-century antiquarianism and Gandalf's tale as paratactic clause-chaining seeded with unfamiliar proper nouns.
claims.quote: paratactic movement from clause to clause

claims.claim: Strider talks colloquially with hobbits but switches to high speech with Boromir, and Elrond's antiquity comes from vocabulary plus inverted grammar.
claims.source: 'Sublimis and Humilis; Aragorn and Strider', Tolkien: Medieval and Modern
claims.quote: a combination of both vocabulary and grammar

claims.claim: Rateliff argues Éowyn's shift to thee/thou marks intimacy, a poetic-diction register modern readers have lost and misread as formality.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Eowyn's Thee and Thou' (Sacnoth's Scriptorium)

claims.claim: Bowman notes the Red Book device puts the tale inside quotation marks, casting Tolkien as translator rather than author.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings'

claims.claim: Forchhammer's analysis of narrative layers includes stylistic shifts between high or epic passages and down-to-earth narration within the chronicler frame.

verdicts.trueWording: Stimpson's charges, rebutted by Patrick Curry
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: Shippey "replies to Colin Manlove's attack on Tolkien's 'overworked cadences' and 'monotonous pitch'". Stimpson's charge "Tolkien's language betrays 'class snobbery'" is also verbatim, in a table captioned "Criticisms of Tolkien by Catherine R. Stimpson, rebutted by Patrick Curry". Downgraded because the page names CURRY, not Rosebury, as the rebutter; Rosebury appears only as one who "began to consider why Tolkien had attracted such hostility" and re-evaluated the work. Shippey-as-rebutter is correct.

verdicts.trueWording: the avoidance of words associated with the modern world
verdicts.note: p.2: "the impression of archaicity ... is partly due to three simple lexical causes: the 'overuse' of words borrowed from nineteenth-century fiction, the avoidance of words associated with the modern world, and the comparatively dense use of new coinages, unusual grammatical patterns, rare or obsolescent words." Two minor softenings in the claim: the source says "partly due", and the third cause also covers new coinages and unusual grammatical patterns, not just rare/obsolescent words. Page cite p.2 correct.

verdicts.trueWording: obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing
verdicts.note: p.2 lists exactly four lexical sets: "(1) landscape description; (2) position or direction; (3) warfare and the struggle between good and evil; (4) other descriptive verbs and adjectives." whither, thither, yonder and afar all appear in the cited key-word list. Quote verbatim: "so many of the keywords used to describe its settings were obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing". Page cite p.2 correct.

verdicts.trueWording: borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf
verdicts.note: p.2: "Tolkien borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf (e.g. valour, valiant, corslet), stretching them creatively to cover a wider range of uses than was possible in Old or Middle English (e.g. Branched lightning smote down upon the eastward hills.)" All three example words confirmed. Minor: the passage sits wholly on p.2, not p.2-3 as cited.

verdicts.trueWording: use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns
verdicts.note: p.2: "Tolkien tends to use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns", with smoke as the example -- "a black smoke swirled in the air" -- "a use that is notably infrequent in modern fiction". Descriptive verbs defined as carrying "an additional semantic feature that assumes the function of a manner adverb"; gleam, loom, plod and stride all appear in the key-verb list. Minor: passage is on p.2, not p.3 as cited.

verdicts.trueWording: About half of The Lord of the Rings consists of dialogue
verdicts.note: Rendered page: "About half of The Lord of the Rings consists of dialogue, poetry and song, or stories told by a character. Thomas Kullmann and Dirk Siepmann liken this to the epic poetry of Homer and Virgil..." and "narrative, which frequently takes the point of view of one of the characters, most often - 85% of the time - one of the four Hobbit protagonists". Both figures and the Kullmann/Siepmann attribution confirmed. (Exact-string test in raw wikitext fails only on the '' italic markup around the title.)

verdicts.trueWording: epic style, marking out characters as old-style heroes
verdicts.note: First half verbatim: "Kullmann and Siepmann observe that characters such as Sam Gamgee and Gollum are marked out by their non-standard speech." Second half downgraded: the page says "Other omniscient narrator passages are in epic style, marking out characters as old-style heroes" -- it names NO character there. Aragorn is discussed elsewhere on the page only as having "Archaic, literary" speech; tying him to the old-style-hero sentence is the claimant's inference, not the source's wording.

verdicts.trueWording: The Narrative Syntax of The Lord of the Rings
verdicts.note: Confirmed in the raw Google Books HTML (not just via summarizer). Chapter listing: "Tolkien as a Stylist Key Words and Key Collocations in The Lord of the Rings" (39), "The Narrative Syntax of The Lord of the Rings" (70), "Points of View" (89), "Landscape Descriptions" (128), "Speeches and Declarations" (159), "Storytelling" (193), "Poems and Songs" (227), "Language and Character" (259). Every topic in the claim maps to a separate chapter; "separate stylistic systems" is the claimant's gloss but the structure supports it.

verdicts.trueWording: the various prose styles of English used in writing
verdicts.note: Confirmed in raw CEEOL HTML. Abstract: "His views in phonology and phonaesthetics were applied directly to his invented languages, to his mythology of Middle-earth, and to the various prose styles of English used in writing Lord of the Rings." Author Susan Robbins, Zmogus ir zodis 15/2013, pp.183-191. The claim's "not only to invented languages" is fair: prose styles are a third item in the source's own list.

verdicts.trueWording: like an historian, or a nature writer, or an epic poet
verdicts.note: Verbatim: "the narrative voice will sound like an historian, or a nature writer, or an epic poet, or an antiquarian in turn, depending on the moment." Setting-dependence is explicit -- "the style of any given narrative moment depends upon its environment" -- and the cheerful Shire register is there too: "close to the cheerful travelling companion that we find in The Hobbit". The claim omits the fourth item ("antiquarian") from the list but does not misstate it.

verdicts.trueWording: paratactic movement from clause to clause
verdicts.note: Verbatim: "Note the paratactic movement from clause to clause and the introduction of unfamiliar proper nouns" -- of Gandalf's telling of Isildur and the Ring in "The Shadow of the Past". Antiquarian reading also confirmed: of the Prologue subtitle "Concerning Hobbits", Halbrooks writes "This places the text in the stylistic mode of a certain strain of nineteenth-century English antiquarianism".

verdicts.trueWording: a combination of both vocabulary and grammar
verdicts.note: Verbatim: "As Shippey notes, Elrond's style of archaism is achieved with a combination of both vocabulary and grammar", with "tidings" plus "the inversion of the subject and verb" as the two mechanisms. Strider half confirmed: "Around the hobbits, Strider is able to relate with their manner of speech and can talk very colloquially"; "when presented with a formal situation, Aragorn can quickly switch to a more appropriate style of speech ... speaking directly to Boromir".

Verbatim: "over the course of the last century we've lost 'poetic diction', despite Owen Barfield's best efforts on its behalf." Intimacy reading confirmed: the second usage "was for intimate use: this is how you refer to people you are close to ... an extra layer to Eowyn's laying bare her feelings". The misread-as-formality element is the post's own framing -- "Why, I wondered, did she suddenly switch to formal, archaic English (Bible-speak)" and "Tolkien is trying for one effect and instead achieving another."

Verbatim and correctly attributed: the Red Book frame "effectively puts the whole of The Hobbit, including the troublesome closure, 'inside quotation marks', as Bowman puts it". Two scope notes: the page says it encloses The Hobbit specifically, not "the tale" at large; and the translator-not-author framing ("the claim that he had translated it into English from the original Westron rather than written it himself") sits in the adjoining section cited to Turner, Flieger, Brljak and Kullmann, with Bowman among the cites for the found-manuscript conceit.

verdicts.trueWording: the narration is 'high' or 'epic' ... far more down to earth
verdicts.note: Verbatim, in a post signed "-- Troels Forchhammer": "Occasionally the narration is 'high' or 'epic' while at other times it is far more down to earth. This creates different moods, and should be included." It is item 4) Style in his four-dimension scheme, and the chronicler frame is his own layer -- "as if the chronicler (another of my layers) were paraphrasing the witness". Caveat on weight: this is an unrefereed Usenet post outlining work in progress, not a published analysis.
